items.title: Naval's barbell thesis: AI kills the 'murderous middle', not just jobs
items.idea: Naval Ravikant: "market structure will shift from a fat middle to mega-aggregators and a long tail." AI collapses the cost to build, so aggregators like Google absorb common use cases while a long tail of micro-tools serves the rest — and if AI eats switching costs, the moat that made enterprise SaaS sticky disappears with it.
items.angle: This is the thesis for why mid-cap SaaS multiples keep de-rating while both hyperscalers and tiny AI-native tools re-rate. Check your book for "murderous middle" exposure.
items.tweetA: Naval's framework for AI: not winners and losers, it's a barbell. Mega-aggregators on one end, a long tail of micro-tools on the other. Everyone in the middle — mid-cap SaaS — gets squeezed from both sides at once. That's your 2026 short book.
items.tweetB: If AI collapses the cost of building software to near zero, the thing that dies first isn't the incumbent, it's the switching cost. No moat, no stickiness, no 8x ARR multiple. Look at every $500M-$5B SaaS name in your portfolio and ask which side of the barbell it's on.

items.title: OpenAI says Astra may have crossed its own 'Critical' safety threshold
items.idea: OpenAI says its upcoming Astra model may have hit the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework, and is pausing internal work that doesn't meet stronger security controls — the first time a frontier lab has self-reported crossing its own top capability tier.
items.angle: A regulatory/safety catalyst that could accelerate government AI oversight conversations right as OpenAI is trying to IPO.
items.tweetA: OpenAI just told on itself: Astra allegedly crossed the 'Critical' cybersecurity threshold in their own Preparedness Framework. Read that twice — that's the self-imposed line where a model is judged capable of assisting real offensive cyber ops. $MSFT
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating whether OpenAI's valuation makes sense. Nobody's pricing in the tail risk that their own safety framework says a model 'may have hit Critical.' That's not a PR problem, that's a straight line to a Congressional hearing before the IPO roadshow even starts.

items.title: $111M+ confirmed stolen in Coldcard hardware wallet exploit, could top $130M
items.idea: Galaxy Research confirms 1,719 BTC (~$111M) stolen from Coldcard hardware wallet users, with total losses likely exceeding $130M across 25+ attack patterns and 250+ victim reports. Coinkite still won't estimate customer losses.
items.angle: Hardware wallets were supposed to be the "safe" self-custody answer. This breaks that assumption at scale right as institutions lean into self-custody narratives.
items.tweetA: $111M confirmed stolen from Coldcard wallets, likely topping $130M. This was supposed to be the 'not your keys, not your coins' safe harbor. Self-custody just had its FTX moment and almost nobody outside crypto Twitter noticed.
items.tweetB: 25+ distinct attack patterns, 250+ victims, and the manufacturer still won't put a number on total losses. If you're pitching institutions on cold storage as the risk-free alternative to exchange custody, you now have to explain Coldcard.

items.title: Ex-bitcoin miner Firmus raises $2B at $10.5B for APAC AI factories
items.idea: Firmus, a former Bitcoin miner turned AI infrastructure company, raised a fully subscribed $2B strategic equity round at a $10.5B+ valuation with Nvidia, Coatue, Jane Street and Blackstone to fund AI factory buildout across Australia and Asia-Pacific.
items.angle: Another crypto-miner-to-AI-datacenter pivot getting real institutional capital — the power/land arbitrage that made bitcoin mining work is now the same arbitrage funding AI compute in APAC.
items.tweetA: Firmus: bitcoin miner turned AI infra company, just raised $2B at $10.5B with Nvidia and Blackstone in the cap table. The exact same stranded-power arbitrage that built out mining farms is now building AI factories in Australia and Asia. Same playbook, new tenant.
items.tweetB: Every idle megawatt in APAC that used to hash SHA-256 is being repriced as an Nvidia GPU cluster. Firmus's $10.5B mark tells you what that repricing is worth. Watch for more ex-miners doing this conversion — the power contracts are the moat, not the chips.

items.title: Grayscale moves to auto-stake nearly all $1.6B of ETH in its Mini ETF
items.idea: Grayscale filed with the SEC to make staking the default for virtually all of the $1.6B in ETH held in its Ethereum Staking Mini ETF, carving out exceptions only for fees, redemptions, and network requirements.
items.angle: This converts a passive spot-ETH product into a yield-bearing one inside a wrapper regulators haven't fully priced — a template every other issuer will copy.
items.tweetA: Grayscale just quietly rewired $1.6B of ETH to auto-stake by default inside an SEC-registered ETF. That's a yield-bearing product hiding inside a spot-ETF wrapper. $ETH holders in TradFi accounts are about to earn staking yield without knowing what staking is.
items.tweetB: The real story isn't the $1.6B, it's the template. Once one issuer gets 'stake by default' through the SEC, every other spot-ETH ETF converts within a quarter. This is how staking yield quietly becomes a TradFi product line.

items.title: CFTC tells prediction markets to drop sportsbook-style odds displays
items.idea: The CFTC sent letters warning regulated prediction market platforms to drop American-style gambling odds display and avoid deceptive listing practices, reinforcing its view that sports contracts are derivatives products, not games.
items.angle: The regulatory ambiguity that let Kalshi/Polymarket-style platforms run sports contracts as "not gambling" is closing — a direct shot at the growth engine of the category.
items.tweetA: CFTC just told prediction markets: stop presenting sports contracts like a sportsbook. If you can't display odds the way bettors expect, you can't compete with DraftKings on UX. This is a slow-motion regulatory strangle on the sports-contract growth engine.
items.tweetB: Every prediction market platform built its user acquisition on feeling like sports betting while legally being a derivatives exchange. The CFTC just said pick one. That's a bigger threat to Kalshi's growth curve than any single lawsuit.

items.title: CLARITY Act slips to September, again
items.idea: The Senate delayed a vote on the CLARITY Act — the market structure bill that would settle CFTC vs SEC jurisdiction over crypto — until September, with Majority Leader Thune calling it "queued up first thing when we come back."
items.angle: Another quarter of regulatory limbo for crypto market structure right as institutional products (staking ETFs, tokenized RWAs) scale ahead of the rules meant to govern them.
items.tweetA: CLARITY Act pushed to September — again. Meanwhile Grayscale is auto-staking $1.6B in ETH and Tether is tokenizing Saudi real estate. The market structure bill keeps slipping while the market structure gets built anyway, rules or no rules.
items.tweetB: Congress moves in quarters, crypto product launches move in weeks. By the time CLARITY actually gets a vote, half the products it's supposed to regulate will already be live and generating revenue. The bill is chasing a moving target.

items.title: Trump Media quietly kills its crypto treasury venture
items.idea: Trump Media is scrapping its CRO treasury venture with Crypto.com and Yorkville and scaling down plans to embed prediction markets directly into Truth Social, per Axios.
items.angle: A high-profile political-crypto crossover unwinding quietly is a tell on how thin actual demand was beneath the announcement-driven crypto-treasury trend of the past year.
items.tweetA: Trump Media just quietly killed its CRO treasury deal and shelved Truth Social prediction markets. The crypto-treasury-company trend has been mostly press releases and stock pops — this is one of the loudest names walking one back before it even launched.
items.tweetB: Watch what happens to every other politically-branded crypto treasury vehicle after this. If the highest-profile one can't make the economics work, the smaller copycats trading on ticker-symbol hype alone are in more trouble than their charts suggest.

items.title: Tether pushes tokenization into Saudi Arabia, starting with real estate
items.idea: Tether is expanding its tokenization business into Saudi Arabia, starting with real estate — its first announced Middle East tokenization push outside its stablecoin business.
items.angle: Gulf sovereign capital is becoming a direct counterparty to stablecoin issuers, not just an LP in venture funds — a de-dollarization-adjacent story worth tracking alongside Gulf gold buying.
items.tweetA: Tether tokenizing Saudi real estate is a bigger story than the ticker suggests. The world's largest stablecoin issuer is becoming direct infrastructure for Gulf capital markets, not just a dollar proxy. That's a different business than USDT issuance.
items.tweetB: Everyone tracks Gulf sovereign wealth buying gold as the de-dollarization signal. Tether building tokenization rails inside Saudi real estate is the other half of that story — Gulf capital building parallel settlement infrastructure, not just diversifying reserves.

items.title: The real story isn't Fed 'credibility', it's bank capital relief
items.idea: Barry Knapp argues markets are overreacting to a Fed "credibility crisis" narrative from Chairman Warsh's press conference while underappreciating the real development: a regulatory relief agenda on bank capital/liquidity requirements that could free up balance sheets and help privatize the Fed's balance sheet.
items.angle: If capital relief lands, it's a structural tailwind for bank lending capacity and credit spreads well before any rate cut — a different trade than the rate-cut consensus.
items.tweetA: Everyone's trading the 'Fed credibility crisis' headline from Warsh's press conference. Knapp says that's noise — the real trade is bank capital relief quietly freeing up balance sheets. $XLF isn't rallying on rate cuts that aren't coming, it's rallying on regulatory math.
items.tweetB: Rate cuts pushed into '27, but bank stocks don't need cuts if capital requirements get loosened first. That's a lending-capacity story, not a discount-rate story — different driver, different duration, different winners.

items.title: Labor flipped from inflation risk to disinflation risk
items.idea: July payrolls, the household survey, participation, and wage growth all point to weak labor supply/demand balance, with low churn suggesting wage deceleration has further to run — the labor market has flipped from inflation risk to disinflationary impulse.
items.angle: If the Fed's mandate focus shifts toward employment risk as Knapp expects, that's a bigger regime change than the next CPI print.
items.tweetA: Knapp's read on the jobs data: labor stopped being an inflation risk and became a disinflationary one. Low churn means wage deceleration isn't done. The Fed's 'inflation-only' focus is about to collide with an employment mandate it's been ignoring.
items.tweetB: Nobody's pricing what happens when the Fed has to pivot from fighting inflation to defending jobs in the same cycle. That's not a soft-landing narrative, that's a mandate-conflict narrative — and mandate conflicts are where policy mistakes happen.

items.title: 40% earnings growth is a base effect, not a run rate
items.idea: Q2 earnings growth of roughly 40% is called unsustainable; a slower rate of change likely compresses the market multiple even as financials/industrials look attractive on positive revisions, margin expansion and a manufacturing renaissance theme, while consumer sectors stay unattractive on weak margins and rich valuations.
items.angle: The multiple-compression risk sits underneath a market at record highs — rotation, not a crash, is the base case here.
items.tweetA: 40% earnings growth is the number everyone's celebrating. It's also the number that guarantees multiple compression the moment growth decelerates — because 40% isn't a run rate, it's a base effect. The market at record highs is pricing the growth rate, not the level.
items.tweetB: The rotation call here is unglamorous but investable: financials and industrials on margin expansion and manufacturing reshoring, consumer discretionary avoided on weak margins at rich multiples. That's not a macro call, that's a sector-selection call hiding inside a macro note.

items.title: Is the productivity boom cyclical, or the start of something secular?
items.idea: Productivity is improving, but whether it's cyclical or the start of a secular capex/tech-adoption boom is unresolved; tech, financials and industrials lead the gains while labor share weakness keeps Knapp cautious about calling it durable — good for shareholders now, but a political risk if labor doesn't participate.
items.angle: This is the AI-capex-vs-labor-share debate in one paragraph — the political-risk framing is the underpriced part.
items.tweetA: Productivity is up. Question nobody's answering cleanly: is this AI-driven capex finally showing up in the numbers, or just a cyclical blip? Knapp's answer — good for shareholders either way, but if labor doesn't participate, it becomes a political problem, not an economic one.
items.tweetB: The AI productivity story usually gets told as bullish-for-margins. The part that gets skipped: if all the gains accrue to capital and none to labor, that's not a sustainable equilibrium — that's an election issue waiting to happen.

items.title: China has an EUV prototype — the 'unbreachable' chip moat just cracked
items.idea: On July 26, The Information revealed China is mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet chip tools and even holds an EUV tool prototype — a capability the West considered sacrosanct. Doomberg has predicted this outcome across four separate pieces since April 2024, arguing sanctions accelerated rather than blocked China's chip independence.
items.angle: The "sanctions failed" narrative isn't new to Doomberg's readers, but the EUV prototype detail is a hard capability marker worth pricing into ASML/Applied Materials competitive-risk timelines.
items.tweetA: China has an EUV prototype. Not DUV — EUV, the lithography tech the West spent a decade treating as an unbreachable moat. Doomberg called this exact outcome in April 2024. The sanctions didn't slow China down, they funded the R&D budget to route around them.
items.tweetB: $ASML's entire valuation rests on EUV being a one-company monopoly for another decade. A Chinese EUV prototype doesn't have to be production-ready to move that multiple — it just has to be credible. This is the scenario nobody stress-tested.

items.title: Support for data centers collapsed from 43% to 21% in one year — and Texas just banned them too
items.idea: Support for data center construction near respondents collapsed from 43% to 21% in one year (Embold/Heatmap survey); Gallup shows 71% opposition, higher than nuclear power opposition ever reached (63% in 2001). Opposition is now bipartisan: New York and Texas both enacted moratoriums within weeks of each other.
items.angle: Texas joining New York is the tell — this was a blue-state NIMBY story until now. If red states start blocking too, there's no "just build it somewhere else" release valve left for the AI buildout.
items.tweetA: Data center support fell from 43% to 21% in twelve months. That's not a slow drift, that's a collapse. And now Texas — the state that exists to say yes to industrial buildout — just paused data centers too. The 'build it in a red state' escape hatch just closed.
items.tweetB: Opposition to data centers is now higher than opposition to nuclear power ever got, even at its peak. If you're modeling AI capex growth off unconstrained land and power availability, you're modeling a political environment that no longer exists.

charts.desc: Polling trend chart: support for local data centers falling from 43% to 21% in a year

items.title: AI doesn't compete with humans for jobs — it competes for energy, like cars did with horses
items.idea: Smith's framework: AI doesn't compete with humans for compute, it competes with humans for energy, the scarce resource both need. Like horses displaced not by inability to pull carts but by land/care costs bid away by cars, humans risk being priced out of energy rather than made obsolete by capability.
items.angle: This reframes the AI-labor debate from "will AI take your job" to "will AI's energy demand make your electricity bill unaffordable" — a more immediate, politically salient risk than job displacement.
items.tweetA: Best AI framework I've read all week, and it's not about jobs: 'the danger isn't that AI renders humans obsolete, it's that AI renders humans too expensive to sustain.' Horses didn't lose their job to cars — they lost the land and feed budget to cars. Humans vs AI is an energy-bidding war, not a skills war.
items.tweetB: Everyone's arguing about which jobs AI replaces. Wrong question. The real constraint is energy, not compute — and energy is fungible between 'run a GPU cluster' and 'keep your lights on.' If AI ever gets valuable enough to outbid households for electricity, that's the actual crisis, not unemployment.

items.title: OIH at a 'critical spot' — head-and-shoulders top or breakout, no in-between
items.idea: Meisler flags OIH (oil services ETF) at a critical technical juncture: a turn down here looks like a head-and-shoulders top, while continuation improves the picture. She notes OIH has underperformed XLE on this entire leg up, a pattern she's flagged repeatedly.
items.angle: OIH's relative weakness to XLE has been a leading tell before — worth watching as an early energy-sector rotation signal ahead of any crude move.
items.tweetA: Meisler's OIH chart is the one to watch this week: turn down here and it's a textbook head-and-shoulders top. She's also been flagging that OIH keeps underperforming XLE on this whole leg — services lagging producers is usually the tell that a rally is running on fumes, not fundamentals.
items.tweetB: If you're long energy on the crude/Hormuz story, don't just watch WTI — watch OIH vs XLE. Services stocks lagging producers into a rally has historically meant the move is priced on spot price hope, not on actual drilling/capex follow-through.

items.title: 4.60% on the 10-year is this week's line in the sand
items.idea: Meisler notes the 10-year yield needs to get back under 4.60% to stay in its recent trading range, after Friday's labor market miss triggered a rally.
items.angle: 4.60% is now the line separating a range-bound bond market from yields breaking out toward the much scarier 6-8% scenarios flagged elsewhere in today's reading (Hanke, Vermeulen).
items.tweetA: 4.60% on the 10-year is the line in the sand this week per Meisler's chart. Stay under it, and we're still range-bound. Break it, and you're validating the Hanke/Vermeulen camp calling for 6-8% yields and a 'global financial reset.' One number, two very different regimes.
items.tweetB: Friday's jobs miss pulled yields down toward the range Meisler's watching. The real test isn't the number today, it's whether 4.60% holds as resistance on the next bounce — that tells you if the disinflation trade or the fiscal-blowout trade wins this quarter.

charts.desc: 10-year yield chart with the 4.60% resistance level marked

items.title: XLF's 10-week rally is actually an insurance rally in disguise
items.idea: Everyone's citing XLF's ten straight up weeks as a "banks are back" story — but strip out the non-bank components and the move is much less impressive; insurance names, not banks, have driven most of the strength.
items.angle: A popular narrative is wearing a bank-index costume — worth separating before extrapolating a credit-cycle bull case from XLF's chart.
items.tweetA: XLF up 10 straight weeks and everyone's calling it a banks-are-back story. Meisler's chart says: no, it's an insurance rally. Strip the non-banks out and the actual banks haven't done much. Don't extrapolate a credit cycle turn from an index that's secretly an insurance ETF.
items.tweetB: This is a classic index-composition trap. XLF looks like a clean 'financials' bet but it's currently being carried by insurance, not lending. If your thesis is bank balance sheet expansion, XLF is the wrong proxy right now — you want the actual bank subindex.

charts.desc: XLF chart annotated with the 10-week win streak

items.title: The clawback clause decides your sign-on bonus more than the headline number does
items.idea: Sign-on bonus clawback terms — full repayment vs pro-rated, 24-month vs 12-month windows, gross vs net repayment — decide the actual value of a "$150K sign-on" more than the headline figure. A new California law effective January 1, 2026 restricts how employers can structure these repayment clauses.
items.angle: A granular labor-market/regulatory data point that quietly shifts negotiating leverage for a whole category of high-comp workers, and a case study in comp regulation moving state by state before it's federal.
items.tweetA: A $150K sign-on bonus with full clawback over 24 months is worth less than a $100K one that's pro-rated over 12 and voided on involuntary termination. Nobody reads the clawback clause. California just made it illegal to structure some of these the predatory way, starting this year.
items.tweetB: Watch California's new signing-bonus clawback law as a template. State-level labor protections for high earners — not just hourly workers — are a trend line. Quant/finance comp negotiation is becoming a legal literacy problem before it's a salary negotiation.

items.title: Qube defers 75% of your bonus into its own funds for 3 years — the deferral schedule is the real comp gap
items.idea: Citadel requires employees to invest half of bonuses above an undisclosed threshold into the Wellington Fund for 3.5 years; Qube defers up to 75% of discretionary bonuses for three years into its own funds; Point72 runs 25% deferral on a three-year vest.
items.angle: These deferral structures are effectively forced reinvestment into the firm's own vehicles — a retention tool dressed as a comp structure, and the dispersion between firms (25% vs 75% deferred) is a huge, rarely-discussed differentiator in real comp.
items.tweetA: Qube defers up to 75% of your bonus into Qube's own funds for three years. Citadel forces half of anything above a threshold into Wellington for 3.5 years. That's not compensation, that's a forced LP commitment with a job attached. The headline comp number and the actual liquid comp number can differ by 2-3x.
items.tweetB: If you're comparing quant fund offers on base + bonus alone, you're comparing the wrong numbers. The deferral structure — what fund it's locked into, for how long, at what vest — is where the real difference in offers lives, and it's the part candidates almost never negotiate.

items.title: Goldman: markets price $19T of future AI revenue. Realistic forecasts see $5-8T.
items.idea: Goldman estimates $27T has been added to global equity value since ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022, pricing in roughly $19T of future AI-driven revenue — while even the most optimistic macro forecasts only point to $5-8T of additional global economic output from AI.
items.angle: The cleanest "AI bubble math" data point of the week — a 2.5-4x gap between what's priced and what's plausible, stated by Goldman's own numbers, not a bear's numbers.
items.tweetA: Goldman's own math: markets are pricing $19 trillion of future AI revenue. The most optimistic economic forecasts only see $5-8 trillion of AI-driven output, total. That's not a bear case, that's Goldman grading its own client base's optimism against its own economists' models.
items.tweetB: $27 trillion in equity value added since ChatGPT launched. Compare that to global GDP (~$105T) — markets have priced in AI adding a quarter of world output's worth of value, and the realistic forecast is a third of that. The gap has to close one of two ways: revenue catches up, or price does.

charts.desc: Valuation scenario chart: $27T equity gain vs $19T priced-in AI revenue vs $5-8T realistic economic forecast

items.title: 68% of Alphabet's Q2 EPS beat was unrealized paper gains, not the actual business
items.idea: On July 22, 68% of Alphabet's reported Q2 EPS came from unrealized gains on its Anthropic and SpaceX holdings — core EPS was actually a slight miss. Anthropic is expected to account for 44% of Google Cloud's FY27 revenue.
items.angle: The "hyperscaler earnings beat" narrative driving the AI stock rally is substantially a mark-to-market accounting effect on private stakes, not operating performance.
items.tweetA: 68% of Alphabet's Q2 EPS beat was unrealized gains on its Anthropic and SpaceX stakes. Core business actually missed. The 'earnings are beating, therefore AI capex is justified' narrative is substantially a mark-to-market illusion on private paper gains, not operating leverage.
items.tweetB: Anthropic is projected to be 44% of Google Cloud's FY27 revenue. Alphabet isn't just an investor in Anthropic anymore, it's structurally dependent on it for cloud growth. That's concentration risk hiding inside a 'diversified' mega-cap, and nobody's pricing it that way.

items.title: Amazon's paper gain on Anthropic alone beat all of global retail plus AWS combined
items.idea: Amazon's $4.25/share paper gain on its Anthropic stake dwarfed combined earnings from global retail and the rest of AWS; Barclays estimates OpenAI and Anthropic together account for around 80% of total AWS AI revenue.
items.angle: Amazon's stock is increasingly a leveraged bet on one company's valuation trajectory wrapped inside a retail conglomerate.
items.tweetA: Amazon's paper gain on Anthropic alone beat combined earnings from global retail plus the rest of AWS. Read that again. $AMZN is quietly becoming an Anthropic-linked structured product with an e-commerce business bolted on for scale.
items.tweetB: Barclays: OpenAI and Anthropic are ~80% of AWS's AI revenue. Not 'contribute to' — ARE. If either lab stumbles, AWS's growth story stumbles with it. The market keeps treating AMZN's AI exposure as diversified. It's a two-name bet.

items.title: Court filings reveal Microsoft put over $100B into OpenAI — a number we only know because of a lawsuit
items.idea: Court filings from the Musk/Altman litigation revealed Microsoft has funneled over $100bn into its OpenAI relationship since inception; over 70% of Azure's AI-related revenue reportedly originates from the two foundation model companies (OpenAI and Anthropic).
items.angle: A rare hard number on Microsoft's actual OpenAI exposure, replacing years of analyst guesswork.
items.tweetA: $100 billion. That's the actual, court-disclosed number for what Microsoft has put into OpenAI since inception — not an analyst estimate, a legal filing from the Musk/Altman lawsuit. We only know this because two billionaires are suing each other.
items.tweetB: 70%+ of Azure's AI revenue comes from OpenAI and Anthropic combined. Microsoft spent a decade diversifying Azure away from any single customer concentration risk, then built its entire AI growth narrative on two customers it also happens to be a major investor in.

items.title: DeepSeek is out-consuming OpenAI and Anthropic combined by 30%
items.idea: Per OpenRouter data, weekly token consumption on DeepSeek exceeded 130% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined.
items.angle: The clearest usage-based (not funding-based) signal that the open-source/cheap-token model is winning actual inference volume, even as the closed labs win the valuation headlines — a divergence that can't persist indefinitely.
items.tweetA: DeepSeek is processing more tokens per week than OpenAI and Anthropic combined — 130% more, per OpenRouter. The two labs commanding $850B and $965B valuations are being out-consumed by the 'free' open-source alternative. Valuation and usage have completely decoupled.
items.tweetB: Everyone models AI winners by funding round size. Nobody's weighting by actual inference volume. On volume, DeepSeek is already the market leader. If enterprises are routing real workloads to the cheap model and reserving the expensive ones for marketing demos, that's the tell the valuations haven't priced in yet.

items.title: 'EBTIT' is this cycle's Community-Adjusted EBITDA
items.idea: OpenAI ($850bn) and Anthropic ($965bn) private valuations have expanded dramatically in 2026. Blind Squirrel dismisses the industry's proposed "EBTIT" metric (earnings before model Training, Interest and Tax) as no more credible than WeWork's Community-Adjusted EBITDA, since training cost is a recurring survival expense, not one-off capex.
items.angle: A sharp, quotable framework for why the industry's preferred profitability metric is a red flag, not a green one.
items.tweetA: The AI labs' new favorite metric is 'EBTIT' — earnings before (model) Training, Interest and Tax. In English: profitable if you ignore the cost of staying competitive. We've seen this movie. It was called 'Community-Adjusted EBITDA' and it starred WeWork.
items.tweetB: Training the next frontier model isn't optional capex, it's the cost of staying in business next year. Any profitability metric that excludes it isn't measuring health, it's measuring how good the story sounds before the next funding round. Anthropic at $965B and OpenAI at $850B are both being sold on exactly this metric.

items.source: ChinaTalk (Jordan Schneider, Justin McIntosh, Roel Konijnendijk)
items.title: Odyssey book sales up 76% YoY off Nolan's film adaptation
items.idea: Sales of Homer's Odyssey are up 76% year-over-year following Christopher Nolan's film adaptation, per the ChinaTalk hosts' closing discussion.
items.angle: A 2,800-year-old text getting a 76% sales bump from a movie is a clean data point on how much cultural attention still converts directly into commerce when a big-budget adaptation lands.
items.tweetA: Odyssey sales are up 76% year-over-year off the back of one Christopher Nolan movie. A poem older than the Roman Empire just got a better sales quarter than most active frontlist releases. Attention-to-commerce conversion on legacy IP is still wildly underpriced by publishers.
items.tweetB: Same mechanic as a 15-year-old novel jumping onto bestseller lists after a Netflix adaptation — except here the 'author' has been dead for 2,800 years and still gets the sales pop. Media tie-in economics work on anything with a recognizable name, no matter how old.

items.title: 26.6% ROIC, zero debt, 4x EV/EBITDA — a stealth pick built on regulation-as-moat
items.idea: An undisclosed $250M market-cap company trades at 4x EV/EBITDA (16.4% FCF yield + 4% dividend) despite a 26.6% ROIC, zero bank debt, and >100% earnings-to-FCF conversion. Incoming regulation raised working capital requirements that crushed smaller leveraged competitors, while this debt-free, majority insider-owned operator absorbed their market share.
items.angle: The setup — regulation as a moat-builder for the strongest balance sheet in a fragmented industry — is a repeatable small-cap pattern worth screening for beyond this specific (undisclosed) name.
items.tweetA: 26.6% ROIC, zero debt, >100% FCF conversion, trading at 4x EV/EBITDA with a 16.4% FCF yield plus a 4% dividend. The market cap is $250M. Somewhere out there is a screen that would have found this before the newsletter did — that's the actual lesson, not the ticker.
items.tweetB: The setup here is the interesting part, not the specific stock: new regulation forces working capital up, kills the leveraged small players, and the one debt-free operator with 50%+ insider ownership just eats their market share. That pattern repeats across industries — go find the next regulatory-hellhole-turned-moat before it's a 4x multiple.

items.title: -23K jobs vs +83K expected — and the S&P closed the week at a record high
items.idea: The US economy lost 23,000 jobs in July against a consensus forecast for +83,000; unemployment slipped to 4.1%; May/June payrolls were revised down a combined 103,000. Traders removed September rate hike bets, yields fell, and the S&P closed the week at a record 7,757.64, up 3.6%, its best week since April.
items.angle: A payrolls miss usually spooks markets — instead stocks rallied hard because it repriced Fed hike odds to zero, showing how thoroughly "bad news is good news" has re-asserted itself.
items.tweetA: -23,000 jobs vs +83,000 expected, plus a 103,000 downward revision to the prior two months — and the S&P closed the week at a record high, up 3.6%. That's not a market shrugging off bad data, that's a market that has fully re-priced to 'bad jobs data = no more hikes.' Bad news is good news, officially back.
items.tweetB: The Fed removed September hike bets on this print. Read the reaction function: three months ago this kind of miss would have triggered a recession-scare selloff. Now it triggers a record close. Same data, opposite market regime — that's how you know positioning, not fundamentals, is driving price.

items.source: Chris Vermeulen (The Technical Traders) via The David Lin Report
items.title: S&P to 8,555, then a blow-off top that leaves latecomers underwater for a decade
items.idea: Chris Vermeulen sets an S&P 500 target of 8,555 (~10% upside), calling it the market's "last euphoric push" before a blow-off top. His bigger warning is on bonds: 10/30yr yields toward 8% could trigger a "global financial reset" by crushing overleveraged borrowers.
items.angle: The stock call is bullish near-term but the bond call is the one that matters more — an 8% yield scenario is severe for anything levered, and it's coming from a technician, not a permabear.
items.tweetA: S&P to 8,555 near-term, says Vermeulen — then a blow-off top that leaves late buyers underwater for a decade. That's not a bear call, that's a 'get greedy for one more leg, then get out before everyone else tries to' call. The exit timing is the entire thesis.
items.tweetB: Buried under the bullish S&P target: Vermeulen thinks 10/30yr yields are headed toward 8%, which he calls a 'global financial reset' for overleveraged borrowers. Nobody's pricing 8% yields into anything right now. If he's even half right, the equity blow-off top and the bond reset happen in the same window.

items.source: Steve Hanke (Johns Hopkins) via The David Lin Report
items.title: First US yen intervention since 1998 — funded by selling euros to avoid looking dollar-weak
items.idea: The US and Japan jointly intervened to defend the yen near a 40-year low of 164/dollar, the first US yen purchase at scale since 1998, funded by selling euros rather than dollars. Hanke's Divisia M4 money supply growth reading has accelerated from 4.6% to 8.5% annualized across the last four quarters, which he reads as building inflation pressure the Fed isn't acknowledging.
items.angle: A first-since-1998 policy intervention plus an accelerating money-supply trend most macro commentary ignores in favor of rate-focused analysis is a genuinely underpriced combination.
items.tweetA: First US yen intervention since 1998, and they funded it by selling euros instead of dollars specifically to avoid looking like they're defending a weak dollar. That's a level of signaling paranoia that tells you more about how fragile the FX picture looks internally than any official statement will.
items.tweetB: Hanke's Divisia M4 growth: 4.6% → 5.6% → 7.5% → 8.5%, accelerating for four straight quarters. Everyone's watching the Fed funds rate. Hanke's framework says rate watchers are looking at the wrong variable entirely — and by his math, inflation pressure is building, not easing, while consensus assumes disinflation.

items.source: David Nicoski (Vermilion Research) via The David Lin Report
items.title: Korea's KOSPI just had its worst month ever — worse than 1998, 2008, or the dot-com crash
items.idea: South Korea's KOSPI fell 33% in July, its worst month on record, worse than the 1998 Asian crisis, 2008 GFC, or the dot-com bust, with roughly 1.2 million accounts (about 3% of the population) margin called before the index rebounded sharply. Meanwhile US tech sits at 42% of the S&P 500's weight and looks "parabolically extended," with SMH down 22-23% from its June peak.
items.angle: A worse-than-1998 crash in a major tech-heavy market barely registered in US headlines — worth checking whether Korean semiconductor supply-chain stress is an early tremor for the broader AI hardware trade.
items.tweetA: Korea's KOSPI just had its worst month ever — worse than 1998, worse than 2008, worse than the dot-com crash. 1.2 million accounts got margin called, 3% of the entire population. This barely made US financial news. If you're long the AI hardware trade and haven't checked what happened to Samsung and SK Hynix in July, you're missing the leading indicator.
items.tweetB: US tech is 42% of the S&P and 'parabolically extended' per Nicoski, with SMH already down 22% from its June high. Korea's chip-heavy market just showed you what a disorderly unwind of an extended tech trade looks like. The US hasn't had its version yet — Korea might be the preview.

items.source: George Noble (Noble Capital Advisors) via The David Lin Report
items.title: Up 439%, then down 67% in a month — Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund blew up on leverage
items.idea: Leopold Aschenbrenner's ~$45B fund was up 439% before four-times leverage erased 67% of its value in a single month, forcing a sale absorbed by Citadel; stripping out its Anthropic stake left him near zero on publicly traded positions. Noble also grouped SpaceX and Tesla as "two of the best shorts in market history," noting SpaceX trades near $1.4T market cap against $7.8B quarterly revenue, with a share unlock the next day lifting float from 5% to 25%.
items.angle: A 439%-to-forced-liquidation collapse from leverage in one month is one of the starkest cautionary tales of the entire AI-trade cycle.
items.tweetA: Up 439%. Then down 67% in a single month from 4x leverage. Forced sale, absorbed by Citadel. That's Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund — one of the loudest AI bulls of the cycle — and strip out his Anthropic stake and he's near zero on everything publicly traded. This is what 'the trade was right, the position sizing wasn't' looks like in real numbers.
items.tweetB: SpaceX: $1.4 trillion market cap against $7.8B quarterly revenue, plus a float unlock from 5% to 25% of shares the very next day. Noble's not calling this an AI bubble in the abstract — he's calling it the best short in market history, with a specific liquidity event as the catalyst. That's a falsifiable call with a date attached.

items.source: Mark Thornton (Mises Institute) via The David Lin Report
items.title: The 'skyscraper curse' comes for AI data centers: $725B in 2026 capex, up 77% YoY
items.idea: 2026 AI infrastructure spending guidance stands at $725B, up 77% from last year. Thornton applies the "skyscraper curse" (the Chrysler Building opened in 1931, the Burj Khalifa in 2010, both right as their financing booms turned to bust) to data centers as the modern equivalent — financed by the same cheap credit but built in rural counties instead of city skylines.
items.angle: A concrete historical pattern-match for AI capex timing risk that's more falsifiable than generic "bubble" talk — worth tracking against actual data center completion dates in 2026-2027.
items.tweetA: $725B in AI infra spend for 2026, up 77% YoY. Thornton's framework: this is the skyscraper curse — the Chrysler Building opened in 1931, the Burj Khalifa in 2010, both right as the credit boom that financed them turned to bust. Data centers are the new record-tower tell, just built in rural counties instead of skylines.
items.tweetB: The skyscraper curse isn't really about height, it's about timing: the building that takes years to finance and construct always opens after the market has already turned. If AI data centers follow the same multi-year build cycle, the ones breaking ground today are scheduled to open right into whatever the AI capex cycle looks like in 2027-2028 — good or bad.

items.source: Joanne Hsu (University of Michigan) via The David Lin Report
items.title: Consumer sentiment has zero correlation with the S&P 500 — and it shows
items.idea: University of Michigan consumer sentiment hit 55.2 in July, up from 49.5 in June but still 11% below year-ago levels. The index shows essentially no correlation with the S&P 500, and sentiment splits sharply by wealth — stock owners feel far better about the economy than non-owners, who barely moved despite record equity highs.
items.angle: The wealth effect from record stocks isn't reaching the median household's sentiment at all, which undercuts any "stocks are up, consumers must feel fine" assumption baked into retail spending forecasts.
items.tweetA: Consumer sentiment index: essentially zero correlation with the S&P 500, per the University of Michigan's own director. Record stock highs, and it's not moving the median consumer's mood at all. If your retail sales forecast assumes a wealth effect from this rally, the data says that channel isn't firing.
items.tweetB: Sentiment splits almost entirely by whether you own stocks. Equity owners: euphoric. Everyone else: barely moved off a historic low. That's not an economy-wide vibe shift, that's a widening gap between asset owners and everyone else showing up in real-time survey data, not just inequality statistics.

items.source: Gary Wagner (TheGoldForecast.com) via The David Lin Report
items.title: Gold confirmed its double bottom at $4,000 — but fell, not rallied, on the Iran strike
items.idea: Gold gapped ~4-5% (~$178) higher to trade near $4,300/oz, confirming Wagner's July 14 double-bottom call at $4,000 with a close above $4,190. He sets resistance at $4,400 and calls $4,000 the line in the sand — a close back below it would mean a multi-year correction, echoing gold's post-2011 fall from ~$1,900 to ~$1,000 by 2016.
items.angle: Wagner explicitly flags he's puzzled gold fell rather than rallied on the US strike on Iran — a break from gold's usual geopolitical-hedge behavior worth noting as a regime-change signal in its own right.
items.tweetA: Wagner called the exact double bottom at $4,000 back on July 14. Gold just gapped 4-5% to confirm it, trading near $4,300 with $4,400 as next resistance. But the detail he can't explain is the real story: gold fell, not rallied, when the US struck Iran. That's not how the safe-haven trade is supposed to work.
items.tweetB: $4,000 is the line: hold it and this is a healthy correction in a bull market, break it and Wagner says you get gold's 2011-2016 replay — a slide from ~$1,900 to ~$1,000, a real multi-year bear, not a dip. One level, completely different decade ahead depending which side it closes on.

items.source: Florian Grummes (Midas Touch Consulting) via The David Lin Report
items.title: Gold's 25-year bull market eyes $5,000; Bitcoin cycle turn pegged to mid-October
items.idea: Grummes calls gold's current move part of a secular bull market roughly 25 years old, with a $5,000/oz retest possible by year-end. Silver is repeating its 1980 and 2011 blow-off-top pattern near $121/oz with support at $45-55. On Bitcoin, he expects a cycle turn around mid-October with a three-year target near $300,000, while flagging Michael Saylor's leveraged strategy as an ongoing risk.
items.angle: A specific mid-October Bitcoin cycle-turn call plus a named systemic risk (Saylor's leverage) is a lot more falsifiable than the usual vague crypto-cycle chatter — worth calendaring.
items.tweetA: Grummes' Bitcoin call has an actual date: cycle turn around mid-October, $300K target within three years. He also names the specific risk to that thesis — Michael Saylor's leverage. That's a testable prediction with a named failure mode, which is rarer in crypto commentary than it should be.
items.tweetB: Gold's bull market is 25 years old and Grummes sees a possible $5,000 retest by year-end. Silver's doing its third replay of the exact same 1980/2011 blow-off pattern near $121. If you've traded silver through the last two of these tops, you already know how this chapter usually ends — the pattern-recognition trade here isn't subtle.
